topic: Proof of Snell's Law via Fermat's Principle
target_audience: First-year university physics students or advanced high school students

sections.title: The Hook: The Lifeguard's Dilemma
lecture_lines: A lifeguard must reach a swimmer as fast as possible.
Running on sand is faster than swimming in water.
The quickest path isn't straight, but Fermat's way.
animations: Draw background: top half #C2B280 (sand), bottom half #0077BE (water). Place Point L (#FFFFFF) at top-left and Point S (#FFFFFF) at bottom-right.
Display vector arrow in sand labeled 'v_sand' (#FFD700) and a shorter vector arrow in water labeled 'v_water' (#1E90FF).
Draw a straight dashed line from L to S (#888888). Overlay a solid path (#00FF00) that bends at the interface to spend more distance on sand.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Index of Refraction
lecture_lines: Light travels slower in dense media like water.
The index of refraction, n, defines this speed reduction.
Speed v equals speed of light c divided by n.
animations: Draw horizontal white line (#FFFFFF). Color upper region light blue (#87CEEB) and lower region cyan (#E0FFFF). Light ray (yellow #FFFF00) enters from top.
Label upper region 'n1' and lower region 'n2' (#FFFFFF). Display text 'n2 > n1' indicating higher density.
Display equation 'v = c / n' (#00FF00) in a central box. Highlight 'v' and 'n' as inversely proportional.

sections.title: Geometric Setup of the Boundary
lecture_lines: Let point A be in air and B in water.
Light hits the interface at a variable point x.
Vertical heights are a and b; horizontal distance is d.
Path L1 connects point A to the interface.
Path L2 connects the interface to point B.
animations: Draw horizontal line (#FFFFFF). Place Point A (#FFFF00) at (0, a) and Point B (#FF00FF) at (d, -b).
Place point P (#00FFFF) on the interface. Label the horizontal distance from the origin to P as 'x'.
Draw dashed vertical lines from A and B to the interface. Label heights 'a' (#FFFF00) and 'b' (#FF00FF). Label total width 'd' (#FFFFFF).
Draw solid line segment from A to P and label it 'L1' (#FFFF00).
Draw solid line segment from P to B and label it 'L2' (#FF00FF).

sections.title: The Time Equation Construction
lecture_lines: Total time is distance divided by speed in each medium.
We use Pythagoras to find lengths L1 and L2.
Time T(x) equals L1/v1 plus L2/v2.
animations: Display formula 'Time = Distance / Speed' (#00FF00) at top.
Show equations 'L1 = sqrt(x^2 + a^2)' (#FFFF00) and 'L2 = sqrt((d-x)^2 + b^2)' (#FF00FF) near their respective triangles.
Write 'T(x) = L1/v1 + L2/v2' (#00FF00) at the bottom, substituting the square root expressions.

sections.title: Calculus: Minimizing the Path
lecture_lines: Fermat's Principle states light minimizes the travel time.
We find the derivative of T with respect to x.
Setting the derivative to zero finds the minimum time.
Apply the chain rule to the square root terms.
This gives the equilibrium condition for the path.
animations: Display 'Fermat: dT/dx = 0' (#FFD700) in center screen.
Write the full derivative expression for T(x) with respect to x using the square root terms (#FFFFFF).
Show the derivative set to zero: '1/v1 * d/dx(L1) + 1/v2 * d/dx(L2) = 0' (#FFFFFF).
Perform calculus step: 'x / (v1 * sqrt(x^2+a^2)) - (d-x) / (v2 * sqrt((d-x)^2+b^2)) = 0' (#FFFFFF).
Simplify to equilibrium condition: 'x / (v1 * L1) = (d-x) / (v2 * L2)' (#00FF00).

sections.title: The Geometric Substitution
lecture_lines: Look at the triangles formed by the light path.
The ratio x over L1 is sin(theta 1).
Ratio (d minus x) over L2 is sin(theta 2).
Substitute these sines into our derivative equation.
We get sin(theta 1)/v1 equals sin(theta 2)/v2.
animations: Focus on the geometry. Highlight angle theta1 (#FFFF00) at Point A and theta2 (#FF00FF) at Point B relative to the normal.
Display 'sin(theta1) = x / L1' (#FFFF00) next to the first triangle.
Display 'sin(theta2) = (d-x) / L2' (#FF00FF) next to the second triangle.
Identify the terms 'x/L1' and '(d-x)/L2' in the previous derivative equation: '(1/v1) * (x/L1) = (1/v2) * ((d-x)/L2)'.
Substitute sines to get 'sin(theta1) / v1 = sin(theta2) / v2' (#00FF00).

sections.title: The Final Reveal: Snell's Law
lecture_lines: Replace speeds v with c over refractive index n.
The constant speed of light c cancels out.
Result: n1 sin(theta 1) equals n2 sin(theta 2).
animations: Substitute v1 = c/n1 and v2 = c/n2 into the equation to get '(sin(theta1))/(c/n1) = (sin(theta2))/(c/n2)' (#FFFFFF).
Rewrite as '(n1 * sin(theta1)) / c = (n2 * sin(theta2)) / c'. Strike through the 'c' terms with red lines (#FF0000).
Display final law: 'n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2)' in large, glowing gold text (#FFD700).
